With the same rule the odor map gets {o} region labels and the structure map only {s}.
params.title: Map settings
params.text: Both maps are UMAP projections to two dimensions with a fixed random seed. Three settings of UMAP's two key parameters (number of neighbors, minimum distance) were tried: (15, 0.1), (30, 0.3) and (50, 0.5). The choice used the validation set only, by the share with at least one common label. The structure map, the control, takes its best setting, so that it also performs at its best. For the odor map, (15, 0.1) scored slightly higher on validation (0.755 vs 0.746), but it pulls the molecules into thin strands with little clustering, so (30, 0.3) was kept for readability. This choice does not favour the odor map and does not affect the comparison with the structure map. The table shows the validation results; the metrics are explained in 5.3.
params.valid: Validation (at least one common label / mean Jaccard)
results.title: Odor overlap of map neighbors
results.intro: The test: for each of the {n} molecules in the odor predictor's scaffold-split test set, take the {k} nearest molecules with true odor labels on the 2-D map, and compute the share of them that have at least one true label in common with it, and the mean Jaccard overlap of the labels. True labels are only used for this calculation and are not shown on the page. The test set was computed once, after both maps' parameters were fixed.
results.take: The odor map beats the structure map on both metrics, and neither 95% confidence interval of the difference (paired bootstrap, 5,000 resamples) includes 0; both maps are far above random picks ({rnd}). Projecting to two dimensions loses some neighborhood information, more so for structure: from {sh} to {sm} for structure, only from {oh} to {om} for odor.

supp.text: For all {n} molecules of the maps' fit, the share of the {k} nearest neighbors on the map whose main predicted descriptor (the one with the highest predicted probability) is the same: odor map {o}, structure map {s}. This metric favors the odor map by construction, because the odor map is drawn from these very predictions, so it is only a supplement and not evidence for the conclusion.
limits.1: The map shows the odor representation learned by a model, not a measurement of human odor perception.
limits.2: UMAP distorts distances: local neighborhoods are fairly reliable, but long distances and the relative positions of regions should not be interpreted.
limits.3: Odor predictions have errors, and the positions and colors inherit them; errors may be larger for molecules not used in training.
limits.4: The map covers organic molecules only. Small inorganic odorants such as hydrogen sulfide are not included, although they matter in some foods: hydrogen sulfide, for example, is linked to the cooked and sulfurous notes of heated and UHT milk.
limits.5: Colors and positions reflect odor categories only, not odor intensity, thresholds or the actual contribution in a food.
excluded.note: This map uses the same library as the Ingredient & Substitute Finder: {total} organic molecules. {n} non-flavor molecules were removed: inorganic substances without carbon (including inorganic odorants such as hydrogen sulfide, ammonia and sulfur dioxide), organosilicon compounds (e.g. D6 siloxane, a common GC-MS column-bleed impurity), non-volatile substances, and entries that appear in the original data only as mixtures (their odor labels describe the mixture, not a single molecule).

footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: odor predictions come from the graph neural network of this site's odor predictor, trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw odor labels are not redistributed here and the page shows model predictions only. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.
footer.ref: Related work: Lee BK, Mayhew EJ, Sanchez-Lengeling B, et al. A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception. Science 2023, 381(6661): 999-1006. doi:10.1126/science.ade4401. This page borrows the idea, drawn with this site's model predictions and UMAP; it does not show results of that paper.

about.practice: Molecules that differ in structure but smell alike are mainly useful as substitutes: when the original is restricted by regulation, a substitute may be allowed, or may cost less or be more stable. They also help in understanding how odor relates to structure, which gives ideas for flavor optimization and fragrance design.
train.title: How the map takes shape during training
train.intro: The animation below uses models saved during training: each one predicts the 5,072 molecules of the library when the maps were made, and the predictions are projected to two dimensions the same way as above. At epoch 0 the model is randomly initialized and has learned nothing about odor yet; because an untrained network already gives structurally similar molecules similar outputs, the picture is a dozen or so small clumps of mixed colors. In the first two epochs these become a few long mixed bands; after that, molecules of the same color gradually gather, and the sulfurous ones separate first. The last frame is the model used on this site (epoch 26, best on the validation set) and matches the odor map on the tool page exactly. Each point keeps the color of the final model's main predicted descriptor, so you can follow how one group comes together.
train.note: Points move because the model's predictions change, not because the molecules do. To keep consecutive frames coherent, each frame starts from the coordinates of the next one and is then rotated, scaled and shifted as a whole onto it; this only makes consecutive frames easier to follow and does not change the relative positions of the points. The frames are smoothly interpolated. Part of the movement comes from the randomness of the dimensionality reduction itself: projecting the same predictions again moves the points by about 2% of the map width on average. The intermediate states are therefore only a visualization; distances between clusters should not be read precisely.
train.epoch_final: Epoch {n} (the model used on this site)
train.video_label: Animation of the odor map taking shape during training
train.later: After epoch 10 the validation score rises more slowly; it is best at epoch 26, does not improve in the following 20 epochs, and training stops at epoch 46. The predictions, however, still change a little in every epoch, and this change no longer shrinks (see the curve below the video): the learning rate is fixed during training, so the weights keep taking small steps. Many molecules have several descriptors with close probabilities, and the top one switches back and forth: after epoch 10, about a quarter of the molecules change their top descriptor every two epochs. That is why the picture still moves late in training. After epoch 10 a model was saved every two epochs; in the animation such a step takes 1 s, twice as long as the earlier steps, so the speed of the picture matches the number of training epochs.

snap.res-take: The odor map beats the structure map on both metrics, and neither 95% confidence interval of the difference (paired bootstrap, 5,000 resamples) includes 0; both maps are far above random picks (0.387).
